title: 'The agentic era for attacks is coming' - Is the Digital Grid strong enough?
summary: This layer of critical infrastructure could be more vulnerable than you might think. The recent outages and breaches offer major opportunities for cybercriminals to do serious damage in the time of AI.
body_markdown:
When the power grid goes down, life stops. That’s why we protect the power grid as critical infrastructure. But the power grid is not the only player in the story. There’s an invisible layer of infrastructure that rarely gets mentioned — the Digital Grid.


This past week, millions couldn’t fly to their planned destinations. Others couldn’t withdraw cash from their local ATMs. And millions stopped communicating at their workplaces because email was shut down for more than 24 hours.


Essential services came to a halt.


The Digital Grid is an extensive ecosystem that manages thousands of applications, businesses, and how services operate. We typically picture water and the power grid. Iskander Sanchez-Rola, Senior Director of AI and Innovation at Gen, urges us to widen our definition. He coined the Digital Grid as the “new critical infrastructure. It's no longer just about water or electricity. It's about the digital systems that everything else depends on.”


The Digital Grid is the scaffolding our modern economy relies on, but it’s invisible, so it garners less attention.


## All it takes is one slip to create a cyber safety problem


It may be surprising to hear, but the attack wasn’t a group effort. Gen Threats Lab researcher Luis Corrons believes the attack was due to ordinary operational mistakes and not based on a coordinated campaign. “Based on the available information at the moment, I don’t think they’re related,” Corrons said. He agrees that it’s strange that all the attacks happened in one week but is convinced the cause is human error.


For those who are paying attention to the consequences of daily life powered by the Digital Grid, it's important to be aware that even with basic outages, there are risks you need to know. Scammers can take advantage of these chaotic moments to send fake emails or text messages pretending to be the company you are expecting to hear from. If you click on one of these links, that can lead to a fake website where you might enter personal information – personal information that helps a scammer do damage.


And if something more serious, like a coordinated cyberattack, were to happen, that's even more worrying.


## AI turns cracks into openings


Unlike the power grid, the Digital Grid has received less attention as critical infrastructure. That can leave systems more exposed; meanwhile, AI gives hackers new tools to find and exploit weaknesses faster.


“The agentic era for attacks is coming,” Sanchez-Rola said.


This week Google issued a warning that hackers are getting smarter. They are using AI systems to launch cyberattacks before the user has a chance to even make necessary updates to the software. The[Google](https://www.pennlive.com/news/2026/11/google-issues-chilling-warning-says-were-in-the-era-of-autonomous-attacks.html) report asserts that we’ve entered the "era of autonomous attacks."


“The scale completely changes how scams look. They used to be generic, and now they are hyper-personalized at a scale that was completely impossible before,” Sanchez-Rola said.


Those attacks could allow autonomous AI agents to discover vulnerabilities and launch coordinated attacks at machine speed, and attackers could target multiple platforms simultaneously, which could cascade disruptions across several industries.


These attacks leave smaller businesses especially vulnerable: "Small players were always a target, but now they are an easier target than ever, because agents can do all these attacks at a high rate and with increased personalization," Sanchez-Rola said. "If they go after your local gym or the school your kid is going to, it might seem minor, but there's a lot of data there that they can use."


The Digital Grid isn’t new. The threat is evolving. At Gen, we recognize this emerging threat and can and want to bridge the gap.


## The outage ends. The risk to your data doesn’t.


Just because the news cycle ends regarding data breaches or outages, it doesn’t mean your accounts are necessarily safe. Because there's opportunity there and, in the case of breaches, your personal information has already been compromised, you’re at risk for a number of scams. Here’s what you should be aware of:


- **Phishing/smishing/vishing scams:** You’ll receive a text, email, or phone call from a scammer. The scammer could pose as a bank, merchant, or government entity in order to get your card number, PIN, or banking login.
- **Malware:** Malware can come from a download or link, and scammers could record keystrokes and credentials.
- **Account takeover scams:** A scammer takes over your account through personal login and password information and makes unauthorized transactions on your behalf.
- **Identity theft:** Loans, credit cards, and accounts are opened with your stolen identity.
- **Fake fraud alerts:** A scammer will send you a text alert suggesting that there has been fraud on your account. They will request that you call them and then scam you into revealing details about your account information.


## Protection means taking preventive action


Controlling the Digital Grid isn’t in your hands, but you can make it harder for scammers to make you a target. Here are practical and concrete ways to take action:


1. **Keep monitoring your accounts:** Even after the news cycle ends, review recent transactions on your checking and credit card accounts. Accounts can be compromised at any time.
2. **Breach messages should be accessed on the site:** Don’t access a breach or recovery message via text or email. Instead, go to the original source by opening the app or typing in the company address.
3. **Use different and complex passwords:** Be certain to use at least 16 characters in your passwords, including letters, numbers, and special symbols. And don’t be afraid to change them at a cadence that makes sense for you.
4. **Make multi-factor authentication (MFA) your best friend:** With MFA, a password alone won’t allow a hacker to get into your account.
5. **Update software quickly:** Don’t wait days and weeks before you update software. Hackers don’t need that much of a window to get into your accounts.
6. **Freeze your credit:** If you’re in a place where you don’t need additional credit, freezing it will prevent anyone from opening an account in your name.
7. **Review your credit reports regularly:** You’re able to access your credit reports for free once a week through[annualcreditreports.com](http://annualcreditreports.com/) .
8. **Pause before responding to an urgent message:** Be wary of any message that wants you to act now or says that your account will be locked. Call the source directly if you receive this message.
9. **Install scam detection tools:** Being proactive now can help detect scams and identify what’s dangerous.
10. **Report identity theft to the Federal Trade Commission:** Access[identitytheft.gov](http://identitytheft.gov/) to generate a personalized recovery plan. to generate a personalized recovery plan.
11. **Leverage VPN:** When using public Wi-Fi, a secure VPN will help keep your data secure and online activities more private.
